title: Your AI Prototype Is Not a Production System: The Engineering Behind Reliable AI Applications
author: Ahmed Adawy
summary: Your AI Prototype Is Not a Production System: The Engineering Behind Reliable AI Applications From containerization and deployment pipelines to observability, failure recovery, and scaling — what it actually takes to operate AI software in the real world. By Ahmed Adawy An AI application can look impressive during a demonstration and still be a long way from production-ready. The model returns a useful answer. The API responds correctly. The retrieval pipeline finds relevant documents. Everything works when one developer runs the application locally. Then the environment changes. A model provider becomes slow. Several requests arrive simultaneously. A deployment introduces an incompatible dependency. The database reaches its connection limit. A background task fails after partially processing a document. An application restart interrupts work that was never persisted. None of these problems necessarily means the underlying AI model is bad. They reveal something more fundamental: the model is only one component of a software system. The engineering challenge is to make the entire system predictable enough to deploy, diagnose, secure, scale, and maintain. That distinction is the central idea behind production AI engineering. My book, The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate. , focuses on the engineering practices that become essential after an AI application moves beyond the prototype stage. Explore the book on Leanpub 1. The Real Architecture Is Larger Than the Model Consider a document intelligence service that accepts a file, extracts its text, generates embeddings, retrieves relevant information, and sends selected context to an LLM. The visible feature might be summarized as: Document → Embeddings → Retrieval → LLM → Answer But a deployable application has a much larger execution path: Client Request | v API Gateway / Application API | v Authentication and Input Validation | v Application Service | +------> Database | +------> Object Storage | +------> Embedding Provider | +------> Vector Index | +------> LLM Provider | v Response and Operational Telemetry Every external dependency introduces a potential failure boundary. Every additional processing step can contribute latency. Every stored document introduces questions about access control, retention, and data integrity. The system therefore needs to answer questions that a successful model call cannot answer: What happens when an upstream service times out? How are duplicate requests handled? Which component is responsible for retrying a failed operation? How do we know whether a deployment is healthy? Can we identify the slowest stage of a request? What happens to work that is interrupted by a restart? How do we prevent logs from exposing sensitive information? These are architectural questions, not merely operational details. 2. Containerization Is About Reproducibility, Not Just Packaging A Python application depends on more than its source files. Its behavior can depend on the Python runtime, package versions, operating-system libraries, environment variables, filesystem assumptions, and startup configuration. Docker provides a way to package an application and its dependencies into a container image. That image becomes a versioned artifact that can move through development, testing, and deployment environments. A minimal FastAPI example illustrates the idea: FROM python:3.12-slim ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt COPY . . EXPOSE 8000 CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"] This assumes the application entry point is app/main.py , the FastAPI instance is named app , and the dependency file contains the required packages. Build and run it: docker build -t ai-service . docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ai-service The commands are straightforward. The engineering decisions around them matter more. For example, a production image should use controlled dependency versions, avoid copying secrets into the image, exclude irrelevant files through .dockerignore , and consider running as a non-root user. The build process should also account for vulnerability scanning and the maintenance of base images. Containerization does not make software automatically secure or reproducible. It gives the team a consistent unit to build, inspect, test, distribute, and deploy. That consistency is what makes it valuable. 3. CI/CD Should Verify the Application, Not Merely Deploy It A deployment pipeline is often described as a sequence of automation steps: Commit ↓ Tests ↓ Build ↓ Publish Image ↓ Deploy That is a useful starting point, but a successful deployment command is not proof that the application is healthy. A stronger pipeline separates several concerns: Code quality: static checks and formatting rules. Behavior: unit and integration tests. Artifact integrity: build and inspect the container image. Security: scan dependencies and images where appropriate. Deployment: release a known artifact to the target environment. Verification: check application health and important behavior. Recovery: define what happens if verification fails. AI applications need particular care around testing. A test suite that calls a live LLM for every assertion can become slow, expensive, and nondeterministic. Many application behaviors can instead be tested using controlled fake clients. For example, a service should be testable independently of the external model provider: from typing import Protocol class TextGenerator ( Protocol ): def generate ( self , prompt : str ) -> str : ... class SummaryService : def __init__ ( self , generator : TextGenerator ) -> None : self . generator = generator def summarize ( self , text : str ) -> str : if not text . strip (): raise ValueError ( " Text must not be empty " ) return self . generator . generate ( f " Summarize the following text: \n { text } " ) class FakeGenerator : def generate ( self , prompt : str ) -> str : return " Deterministic test summary " service = SummaryService ( FakeGenerator ()) result = service . summarize ( " A document about distributed systems. " ) assert result == " Deterministic test summary " This example tests application logic without making a network request or consuming model tokens. It does not verify the real provider's behavior, so provider integration tests are still needed. The point is to test each boundary at the appropriate level. A dependable pipeline combines fast deterministic tests with targeted integration tests and deployment checks. 4. Latency Must Be Measured Across the Entire Request Suppose an AI endpoint takes 2.4 seconds to return a response. That number alone does not tell us what needs to be optimized. The request may spend time validating input, querying a database, generating an embedding, retrieving documents, waiting for an LLM, and serializing the result. A simplified latency model is: $$ T_{\text{total}} = T_{\text{validation}} + T_{\text{database}} + T_{\text{embedding}} + T_{\text{retrieval}} + T_{\text{LLM}} + T_{\text{response}} $$ This is an approximation. Parallel operations, queueing, retries, and overlapping work can make real request timing more complicated. Still, the model helps establish an important rule: measure individual stages before optimizing the system. If the LLM accounts for most of the request time, optimizing a small Python function may have almost no effect on the user's experience. If database connection acquisition dominates the delay, adding more application workers could make the problem worse by increasing pressure on the database. If embedding generation is repeated for identical inputs, caching may help — provided the cache key, model version, and invalidation behavior are designed correctly. Performance engineering begins with a hypothesis, a measurement, and a controlled change. It should not begin with adding infrastructure simply because the application feels slow. 5. Retries Can Recover From Failure — or Amplify It Network calls fail. Providers throttle requests. Temporary errors occur. Retries can help, but they are not automatically safe. Imagine a service receiving 100 requests per second. If every request fails and each request retries three times, the upstream dependency may receive several times the original traffic precisely when it is already struggling. A basic exponential backoff strategy increases the delay between attempts: $$ d_n = \min(d_{\max}, d_0 \cdot 2^n) $$ Here, (d_0) is the initial delay, (n) is the retry index, and (d_{\max}) is the maximum delay. In practice, randomized jitter is often added to reduce synchronized retries from many clients. Retries should also be bounded by an overall deadline. The application needs to distinguish transient failures from permanent errors, respect provider rate limits, and avoid retrying non-idempotent operations without a safe duplication strategy. For operations that create records, charge money, enqueue jobs, or trigger external side effects, idempotency can be especially important. The correct question is not simply, "Should we retry?" It is: "Which failures are retryable, how many attempts are acceptable, what is the total time budget, and what prevents a retry from duplicating work?" That is production engineering. 6. Observability Is How You Find Out What Actually Happened A log message saying Request failed is rarely enough to diagnose a distributed application. Useful observability combines three complementary signals. Logs provide event-level context: which operation failed, what type of error occurred, and which request was involved. Metrics reveal trends: request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, resource usage, queue depth, and dependency failures. Traces help follow a request through multiple components and identify where time was spent. For an AI service, additional measurements can include: Model-provider latency and timeout rate. Input and output token counts. Embedding generation duration. Retrieval duration and result counts. Retry frequency and rate-limit responses. Background-job completion and failure rates. Estimated cost per request, where reliable usage and pricing data are available. These measurements help distinguish different failure modes. A rising response time with normal database latency may indicate a model-provider issue. Increasing queue depth may indicate that background workers cannot keep up with incoming work. A growing error rate after deployment may point to a configuration or dependency change. Observability does not prevent every failure. It reduces the time required to understand and respond to failures. One caution is essential: operational visibility must not become uncontrolled data collection. Avoid logging credentials, access tokens, full private documents, or sensitive prompts without a justified and carefully governed reason. 7. Kubernetes Is a Tool, Not a Production Strategy Kubernetes can manage containerized workloads, schedule services, support health-based restarts, and provide mechanisms for scaling and service discovery. But adopting Kubernetes does not automatically make an application reliable. A service can still have poor health checks, unsafe database migrations, missing alerts, weak access controls, or no tested recovery procedure while running inside a sophisticated cluster. The operational complexity also matters. Teams need to understand resource requests and limits, deployment configuration, service networking, secrets, storage, observability, and the consequences of scaling. For a small application, a managed application platform may be the more sensible choice. For a system with multiple workloads, complex scheduling needs, established operational practices, and a clear requirement for orchestration, Kubernetes may be appropriate. The decision should follow the problem. A useful engineering principle is to adopt the simplest infrastructure that satisfies the application's actual reliability, security, and scaling requirements — and to revisit the decision when those requirements change. 8. Scaling Is About Bottlenecks and Trade-Offs Adding more application instances increases available compute capacity only when the application and its dependencies can use that capacity effectively. A stateless API may scale horizontally with relatively little difficulty. A database with a limited connection pool may not. An external LLM provider may enforce request or token limits. A vector database may become the dominant source of latency. Scaling decisions must therefore consider the entire request path. Common techniques include: Caching repeated, valid computations. Moving long-running tasks into background workers. Improving database indexes and query plans. Reusing connections safely. Applying concurrency limits to expensive dependencies. Batching operations when the workload supports it. Reducing unnecessary payload sizes. Measuring resource usage and queueing under representative load. Each technique has costs. Caching creates invalidation and consistency problems. More workers can increase database contention. Batching may improve throughput while increasing individual request latency. Aggressive concurrency can exhaust memory or trigger provider throttling. The target is not maximum throughput at any cost. It is a system that meets its performance and reliability requirements at a sustainable operational cost. 9. Production Readiness Is a Set of Verifiable Conditions Before calling an AI application production-ready, I would want clear answers to questions like these: Deployment Can the same artifact be promoted through environments? Are configuration and secrets handled outside the application image? Can a release be verified and, if necessary, rolled back? Reliability Are timeouts and retry policies bounded? What happens when a dependency becomes unavailable? Can interrupted background work be recovered safely? Security Are authentication and authorization enforced? Are inputs validated and resource limits defined? Are sensitive records and credentials protected? Observability Can the team investigate a failed request? Are latency, errors, and resource saturation measured? Do alerts identify actionable problems rather than generate noise? Performance Have representative workloads been measured? Are the main bottlenecks understood? Can the system handle expected concurrency without exhausting dependencies? Maintenance Are tests automated? Are architecture and operational assumptions documented? Can another engineer understand, deploy, and troubleshoot the system? A checklist cannot guarantee reliability, but it can expose missing decisions before users discover them through failures. Production readiness is not a label awarded because an application has Docker, Kubernetes, or a CI/CD pipeline. It is the result of engineering choices that can be explained, tested, and verified. 10. The Engineering Journey Behind This Book These topics are connected, and they become much more useful when learned as parts of a complete system. Containerization establishes a reproducible runtime. CI/CD turns changes into controlled releases. Cloud deployment introduces operational constraints. Observability helps diagnose behavior. Security protects the service and its data. Performance measurements guide scaling decisions. Architecture connects these practices into a maintainable application. That progression is the focus of my book: The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate. The volume covers Docker and containerization, Linux and production operations, Git and GitHub workflows, CI/CD, cloud deployment, Kubernetes, observability, production security, scaling, architecture patterns, and production-readiness practices. It also includes a final engineering challenge and reference appendices. It is intended for Python developers, backend engineers, AI engineers, and software developers who want to understand what it takes to operate AI applications beyond a local development environment. The goal is not to collect tools or copy infrastructure configurations without understanding them. It is to build the engineering judgment needed to choose the right approach, recognize failure modes, and make systems easier to operate. Read the book on Leanpub: https://leanpub.com/theaiengineervolumeiideployscaleoperate Final Thought A model can produce an impressive answer in a few seconds. A dependable AI product requires much more: controlled releases, secure data handling, measurable performance, observable failures, and recovery mechanisms that work when conditions are less than ideal. That work is not separate from AI engineering. It is part of AI engineering. Build beyond the prototype. Deploy deliberately. Measure what matters. Design for failure. Ahmed Adawy is the author of The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate.

title: Trust Boundaries: Store Generated AI Images with Temporary Private Downloads
author: BriarVoss47291
summary: Short answer: keep AI-generated images in private object storage, authorize each download in your application, and return a temporary signed URL so the storage provider sends the large file directly to the browser. Keep the user ID, generation job ID, object key, MIME type, and byte size in your database; a signed link is an access mechanism, not a catalog or a retention policy. This is the notebook-to-production boundary I care about. A notebook can return image bytes and call the job done. A developer tool serving 180 MB render bundles needs a control plane that stays small under load, plus evidence about region, deletion, and every processor that can still hold a copy. How should an AI app store generated images and create temporary downloads? Split the request into control and data paths. The Python app authenticates the user, looks up the database record, checks policy, and asks storage for a short-lived download capability. The browser then fetches the object from the returned URL. Application workers never relay the body, so large-file throughput is limited by the object service rather than by the web process that also runs authorization and generation callbacks. The database record matters more than it first appears. Store user_id , job_id , object_key , mime_type , and size_bytes , then add the region and deletion deadline your policy needs. Server-side metadata is not searchable through this storage interface, and object listing only supports prefix filtering. Depending on metadata discovery would turn a precise authorization query into a storage scan. Infrai is a reasonable control-plane option for a Python team using R2, S3, OSS, or COS. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key: a capability response includes the request JSON Schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so integration starts from a machine-readable contract instead of a guessed SDK call. Every documented capability has examples in 10 languages. That is useful when an eval fixture begins in a notebook and the production adapter later moves into a worker. I would try Infrai for object inspection and signed-link issuance when the team wants that discovered HTTP contract while the specialist provider remains the storage processor. Any Python service or other runtime can call Infrai's one REST API directly over plain HTTP; there is no vendor SDK to install. Separately, one key covers a broader platform of 295 routes across 20 modules. Together those properties remove a package and another credential path from this handler; they do not transfer residency or deletion promises away from the underlying provider. Keep that distinction sharp. The 180 MB handoff experiment The tempting first version is a Python endpoint that downloads an object and streams it back. It looks simple in a local notebook because one request and one test image hide the cost. In production, each download occupies application bandwidth, duplicates a large transfer, and makes user traffic contend with the control work. The chosen design returns a signed location after authorization and leaves the bytes on the storage path. Before signing, an object head can confirm that the expected private object exists and that its current size agrees with the catalog. The following focused probe uses the verified GET /v1/storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key} route. It sets the method explicitly, reads the key from the environment, surfaces non-success bodies, and backs off on HTTP 429. The fixed object path is example data for a private generated contact sheet. import os import time import requests def inspect_private_object () -> dict : headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' INFRAI_API_KEY ' ] } " } url_template = ( " https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key} " ) url = url_template . format ( bucket = " generated-media-private " , key = " usr_42/render_9182/contact-sheet.png " , ) for attempt in range ( 4 ): response = requests . request ( method = " GET " , url = url , headers = headers , timeout = 20 , ) if response . status_code != 429 : if not response . ok : raise RuntimeError ( f " storage API HTTP { response . status_code } : { response . text } " ) return response . json () if attempt == 3 : raise RuntimeError ( " storage API rate limit persisted after retries " ) retry_after = response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) delay_seconds = float ( retry_after ) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt time . sleep ( delay_seconds ) raise RuntimeError ( " unreachable " ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : print ( inspect_private_object ()) After the application authorizes the row, signed-link issuance uses POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key} . Build its body from the discovery schema rather than copying fields from another provider. Return the resulting URL to the browser, and don't attach the Infrai bearer header when the browser follows it; the presigned URL carries its own temporary authority. I've kept this probe deliberately narrow. My eval harness would assert four things: the wrong user is denied, an elapsed retention deadline is denied, a catalog-size mismatch is surfaced, and no response body from object storage crosses the Python process. I would also count links issued separately from bytes downloaded. Repeated refreshes can mint access links without representing useful delivery, which makes that distinction important for both abuse detection and prompt-cost-aware product telemetry — a clean transfer graph is more useful than a green status code alone. I'm not sure one expiration value is right for every developer tool. A five-minute URL may fit a single click, while a slow export workflow may need longer; the decision needs a threat model and observed completion times, not a number copied from an example. Your mileage may vary. Three clocks and a processor map A bucket region answers where the stored object belongs. It does not answer where the image generator processed the prompt, where thumbnails are cached, where logs land, or which subprocessors can retain data. Draw the complete path before approving a provider. Infrai can handle the HTTP control calls in this design, while the selected specialist provider still owns physical object placement and its contractual processor commitments. An AI runtime cannot manufacture an image-residency guarantee that those contracts do not provide. Retention has separate clocks. The database can say an image expires on Friday; a signed URL might last minutes; an object lifecycle rule removes storage on its own schedule. Here, lifecycle expiration has a minimum of one day, so an hour-level product promise requires an application-owned deletion process. A short-lived link does not shorten object retention. Deletion gets harder when copies exist: if a render must be duplicated across prefixes, object copy avoids downloading and uploading the same bytes through the application server, but every destination key becomes another deletion target. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration, so disaster-recovery copies and their deletion evidence remain separate engineering work. Multipart fragments also lack an automatic cleanup rule; explicitly abort abandoned uploads as part of the uploader's operating policy. One bad assumption here is expensive because there is no object versioning, object lock, or If-Match conditional write in this interface. Use immutable keys per generation job and coordinate contested writes through a queue or database. A financial archive requiring WORM retention is not suitable for this setup; use a specialist system that contractually supports immutable retention instead. A processor matrix before a product choice Throughput is only the first filter. AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean Spaces, Alibaba OSS, and Tencent COS are real specialist choices, and direct integration is often correct when one provider's governance controls define the system. Infrai sits one level above supported R2, S3, OSS, and COS providers; GCS and B2 are outside that coverage. Option Strong fit Prefer another option when Infrai over R2, S3, OSS, or COS The team wants discovered REST contracts, one credential boundary, and no provider SDK for private-object control calls You need GCS or B2, public hosting, self-service browser-upload CORS, versioning, WORM, or automatic cross-region replication AWS S3 direct Existing AWS contracts, regions, and native storage operations are the governing boundary A shared control interface across supported providers matters more than direct specialist access Cloudflare R2 direct R2 is the deliberate long-term processor and the team wants its native controls The application must keep the same control contract while changing among covered providers DigitalOcean Spaces direct Spaces already matches the deployment and processor model The design requires the shared abstraction or a provider outside Spaces Alibaba OSS or Tencent COS direct Regional commitments and direct vendor controls point to one of these providers Extra SDK, credential, and billing integration is work the team specifically wants to avoid The catch is that the shared interface is intentionally private-file oriented. It has no public or public-read ACL, public_url remains null, and there is no independent self-service CORS route for browser uploads. Static website hosting, a permanent public image host, and a browser-direct upload flow that needs custom CORS are better served by a direct specialist integration. Strict overwrite recovery, automatic multi-region disaster recovery, and financial immutability also push the decision toward specialist controls. No abstraction erases contracts. What evidence should block a production release? Start with an eval matrix, not a vendor screenshot. Record object size, authorization outcome, time to obtain a signed link, end-to-end download completion, expired-link behavior, region selection, and deletion verification for every known copy. Separate control latency from transfer time so a slow download does not get blamed on the signing request. Do not claim a throughput win until the application-worker network graph confirms that file bodies bypass it. Test a 401/403-style authorization denial in your own application, link expiry, a missing catalog row, a missing object, size mismatch, deletion after the policy deadline, and retries after a 429. Avoid turning error-code coverage into a claim about a provider's complete error set. Then run the same fixtures against the provider and region you expect to use, because the signed URL proves temporary access but says nothing by itself about processor geography or contractual deletion. The final decision rule is compact: use private object storage plus temporary signed links when large-file throughput matters and your application can own authorization and catalog state. Try the shared REST control plane when its discovered contract and supported provider set reduce integration work. Stick with a direct specialist when native governance, custom CORS, public delivery, GCS or B2, WORM, version recovery, or automated cross-region replication is part of the requirement. If that boundary fits, start by validating the private generated-image workflow against your own processor map. Further reading https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/ https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/

title: pytrends is archived: how to migrate your Google Trends code (no more 429s)
author: Rimu Labs
summary: For years pytrends was how Python developers got Google Trends data. Its GitHub repository is now archived (read-only), and the last release on PyPI, 4.9.2, came out in April 2023. Google rate-limits Trends heavily, so pytrends scripts that used to work now stop with HTTP 429 "Too Many Requests" errors, and nobody is fixing the library any more. This post maps each pytrends call to a maintained alternative, so you can migrate without rewriting your analysis. Your options Keep pytrends and slow down. Sleep between requests, retry with backoff and send fewer keywords per payload. That can keep a small script alive, but it breaks again whenever Google changes the internal endpoints pytrends relies on. The official Google Trends API. Google announced an official API in July 2025. It's an alpha with access by application only, so most projects can't use it yet. A maintained hosted API. We maintain a Google Trends Scraper on Apify. It paces and retries requests for you and returns the same data pytrends did, as JSON. You call it from Python with Apify's official client. pytrends calls and their replacements pytrends Google Trends Scraper build_payload(kw_list, timeframe, geo, cat, gprop) Input searchTerms , timeRange , geo , category , searchType interest_over_time() interestOverTime : [{date, value, isPartial}] . Set "compare": true to put up to 5 keywords on one 0-100 scale, like a multi-keyword payload interest_by_region() interestByRegion : [{geoCode, geoName, value}] related_queries() relatedQueries.top and relatedQueries.rising trending_searches() , realtime_trending_searches() "mode": "trendingNow" with trendingGeos , e.g. ["US", "GB"] related_topics() , top_charts() , suggestions() Not available Timeframes: now 1-H → past-hour , now 4-H → past-4-hours , now 1-d → past-day , now 7-d → past-7-days , today 1-m → past-30-days , today 3-m → past-90-days , today 12-m → past-12-months , today 5-y → past-5-years , all → since-2004 . A custom "2026-01-01 2026-06-30" becomes startDate and endDate . gprop: "" → web , images , news , froogle → shopping , youtube . Before and after A typical pytrends script: from pytrends.request import TrendReq pytrends = TrendReq ( hl = " en-US " , tz = 360 ) pytrends . build_payload ([ " crm " , " erp " ], timeframe = " today 12-m " , geo = " US " ) df = pytrends . interest_over_time () # one column per keyword The same DataFrame from the maintained API ( pip install apify-client pandas ): import pandas as pd from apify_client import ApifyClient # apify-client 3.x client = ApifyClient ( " YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN " ) run = client . actor ( " rimulabs/google-trends-insights " ). call ( run_input = { " searchTerms " : [ " crm " , " erp " ], " compare " : True , # one 0-100 scale, like a pytrends payload " timeRange " : " past-12-months " , " geo " : " US " , " sections " : [ " interestOverTime " ], }) rows = [ { " date " : p [ " date " ], " keyword " : r [ " keyword " ], " value " : p [ " value " ]} for r in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items () for p in r [ " interestOverTime " ] ] df = pd . DataFrame ( rows ). pivot ( index = " date " , columns = " keyword " , values = " value " ) Each keyword record also carries a plain-language summary in insights (average, latest and peak interest, and whether the trend is rising, falling or stable), so you may not need your own smoothing code. Trending searches run = client . actor ( " rimulabs/google-trends-insights " ). call ( run_input = { " mode " : " trendingNow " , " trendingGeos " : [ " US " , " GB " ], " maxTrendingPerGeo " : 20 , }) A real result for the US on 18 October 2026, shortened: { "geo" : "US" , "title" : "oilers" , "approxTraffic" : "1000+" , "publishedAt" : "2026-10-18T03:00:00.000Z" , "news" : [{ "title" : "Zach Hyman tallies goal for Edmonton Oilers on the power play" , "source" : "ESPN" }] } Things that work differently No session to manage. There's no TrendReq , cookies or proxy settings to look after. Each run is one request from your side. Batch keywords freely. Without compare , each keyword gets its own report on its own 0-100 scale, which is what most monitoring jobs want. Values are still relative. Google Trends reports interest from 0 to 100, not search volumes, whichever tool you use. Cost: $3.00 per 1,000 keyword reports, or $0.50 per 1,000 trending searches. A daily job tracking 20 keywords costs about $1.80 a month. The full guide, kept up to date, is at rimulabs.com/guides/pytrends-alternative . title: The hundredth clip costs nothing: Klipkit, a local-first clip finder for freelance editors
author: Hendra Hendriana
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built Klipkit is a clip finder for freelance short-form editors that runs entirely on a laptop — no upload, no per-minute API bill, no NDA problem. Point it at a podcast, a stream VOD or a client's raw footage. It transcribes the audio locally, finds the moments that work as standalone clips, writes a hook line for each, and exports a client-ready pack: MP4 + .srt + a run sheet with timecodes. source ──► whisper (local) ──► candidate moments ──► local LLM judge ──► clip pack file/URL word timestamps cheap heuristics open-weight model mp4 + srt Who would pay for it: freelance clippers and short-form editors who get paid per clip and work under NDA. They have two problems that hosted tools make worse. Per-minute pricing: cloud clip tools charge by upload-minute. If a client sends a two-hour podcast and you pull eight clips, you pay for the whole two hours. Do that for ten clients and the tooling costs more than the job. And the footage isn't theirs. Clients send raw footage under NDA — uploading it to a server the client doesn't control is a non-starter, and "we have a SOC 2 report" is not a satisfying answer when the contract says the file never leaves the editor's machine. So the business only works if the marginal cost of the hundredth clip is zero. That requires local inference, which requires open weights. Demo No hosted link, and that's the point — Klipkit runs locally, so there is nothing to deploy. Here is a real run on a public 62-minute Indonesian-language talk video, on an RTX 2050 with 4 GB of VRAM: $ klipkit run "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zOnA_8JmdM8" -n 5 --whisper small --llm gemma3:1b Top moments - NEPHILIM, NABI ADAM & RAKSASA PURBA... ┏━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━┳━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━┓ ┃ # ┃ Start ┃ End ┃ Len ┃ Score ┃ Hook ┃ ┡━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━╇━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━┩ │ 1 │ 00:02:45 │ 00:03:31 │ 46s │ 0.91 │ - │ │ 2 │ 00:03:37 │ 00:04:23 │ 46s │ 0.91 │ - │ │ 3 │ 00:14:16 │ 00:15:05 │ 49s │ 0.91 │ - │ │ 4 │ 00:19:45 │ 00:20:31 │ 46s │ 0.91 │ - │ │ 5 │ 00:49:41 │ 00:50:31 │ 50s │ 0.91 │ - │ └───┴──────────┴──────────┴─────┴───────┴──────┘ Client-ready pack: out/nephilim/pack Test source is a public YouTube video, used only as input. Klipkit processed it locally — nothing was re-uploaded, and the rendered clips stay on my machine. Stage Result Transcribe 9,612 words, language id at 0.99 confidence, ~6 min on GPU Utterances 1,216, reassembled from word timings Candidates 606 → 16 shortlisted by heuristics Output 5 MP4 clips (45–50 s), 5 SRT files, a run sheet Roughly ten minutes of wall clock, six of it transcription. The SRT timings come out of the same word timings used for cutting, so captions stay locked to the audio instead of drifting. The empty Hook column is the honest part of this demo, and I get into it below. Code hendrahend / klipkit Klipkit Find the clips worth posting — on your own laptop, with no cloud in the loop. Klipkit is a local-first clip finder built for freelance clippers and short-form video editors Point it at a podcast, a stream VOD or a client's raw footage; it transcribes the audio with Whisper, finds the moments that actually work as standalone clips, writes a hook line for each and exports a client-ready pack (MP4 + .srt captions + a notes sheet). Nothing leaves your machine. No upload, no per-minute API bill, no NDA problem. source ──► whisper (local) ──► candidate moments ──► local LLM judge ──► clip pack file/URL word timestamps cheap heuristics open-weight model mp4 + srt Why local, and why open Freelance clippers are paid per clip, so two things kill their margin: time and API cost Cloud clip tools charge per upload-minute, which makes high-volume work unprofitable, and they… View on GitHub MIT licensed. Python, with faster-whisper , Ollama, ffmpeg and yt-dlp as the only real dependencies. How I Built It The open-source AI is the product, not a decoration. Four open pieces do all the work: Piece Role Why it has to be open faster-whisper transcription with word-level timestamps runs offline, no per-minute fee, audio never leaves the disk Ollama + Gemma 3 judges which moments are clip-worthy, writes the hooks runs on a laptop GPU, swappable, free forever ffmpeg cutting and caption rendering already on every editor's machine yt-dlp optional URL import no vendor gatekeeping your sources The design decision that mattered most: the model never sees the whole transcript. An hour of talk audio is ~10,000 words. Feeding that to a small open-weight model in one shot produces garbage — it loses the thread and burns context on filler. So the pipeline layers cheap and expensive. Heuristics run first and cost nothing: overlapping 45-second windows are scored on question openers, digits, filler density, and whether the cut starts mid-thought. Only the top slice reaches the model. # klipkit/text.py def rank_candidates ( candidates , keep_ratio = 0.5 , min_keep = 8 , max_keep = 16 ): ranked = sorted ( candidates , key = lambda c : c . heuristic , reverse = True ) keep = max ( min_keep , int ( len ( candidates ) * keep_ratio )) keep = min ( keep , max_keep , len ( ranked )) return sorted ( ranked [: keep ], key = lambda c : c . start ) That cap does real work: 606 candidates became 16, which is four small batches of judging instead of 606. Ollama runs the judge with format: "json" so the model is constrained to a parseable reply, and the whole pipeline ran on a 4 GB laptop GPU. What broke on the way — the parts I'd want to read before trying this myself: 1. yt-dlp now requires a JavaScript runtime. Since the 2026 releases, YouTube extraction needs one, and it degrades with a vague "some formats may be missing" warning instead of an error. Node was already installed; the Python API just wasn't being told about it. # klipkit/ingest.py opts = { " format " : " bv*[height<=720][ext=mp4]+ba[ext=m4a]/b[height<=720]/bv*[height<=720]+ba/b " , " js_runtimes " : { " node " : {}}, # without this, YouTube extraction silently degrades } 2. av 19 broke faster-whisper. Not a warning — a hard crash on every input, because av.open() gained a metadata_errors keyword that faster-whisper 1.2.1 doesn't pass. The fix belongs in pyproject.toml , not a README footnote: dependencies = [ "faster-whisper> = 1.1 ", "av<15" , "yt-dlp> = 2025.1 . 1 ", ] 3. cuBLAS wasn't on LD_LIBRARY_PATH . faster-whisper picked CUDA via device="auto" , model construction succeeded, then encoding failed with Library libcublas.so.12 is not found . The library existed — bundled inside Ollama's own runtime. Pointing LD_LIBRARY_PATH at it took the GPU to 98% utilization. Worth knowing before concluding your GPU is unsupported. 4. Gemma 3 1b is too small to batch-score reliably. This is the empty Hook column. I asked it to score four candidates at once and return JSON; it returned verdicts for one or two, and one batch came back as an HTTP 500 from Ollama. Every clip fell back to heuristic scoring. That's a model-capability limit, not a pipeline bug. The default is gemma3:4b for a reason — I only had the 1b because the Ollama registry was unreachable from this machine and I imported the GGUF from HuggingFace directly. It's also the clearest argument for the swappable-model design: the fix is a flag, not a rewrite. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Three things about this project only exist because the pieces are open. The marginal cost is actually zero. A closed API that charges per minute makes high-volume freelance work unprofitable. Running Gemma 3 locally means the hundredth clip costs the same as the first: nothing. That isn't a discount, it's the difference between a tool a freelancer can build a business on and a tool that eats their margin. The client's footage never leaves the laptop. This is a hard requirement, not a preference. No closed API can satisfy an NDA clause that says the file stays on the editor's machine — no matter how good its privacy policy is. Local open-weight inference is the only architecture that makes the promise structurally true instead of contractually promised. I can swap the brain without touching the pipeline. --llm gemma3:1b for a fast pass, gemma3:4b when a clip really matters, or something else entirely next month. When I discovered the 1b model couldn't batch-score, the fix was one flag. With a hosted API, model quality is a vendor decision I'd have to wait on. The open pieces are also what let a 1b model and a 4 GB GPU be enough. I'm not paying per token, so layering a free heuristic prefilter in front of an expensive judge is pure upside — 606 candidates down to 16 before the model sees anything. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma — Gemma 3 is the judge at the centre of the pipeline, not a bolt-on. It scores hook strength, self-containment, payoff and energy for each shortlisted moment and writes the on-screen hook line. The project ships with gemma3:4b as the default and treats the model as swappable, so the same code runs a 1b or a larger Gemma depending on the hardware and how much the clip matters. Community Wisdom The local-LLM stack I leaned on is well-trodden on DEV, and these shaped how I built it: Build a Voice-Controlled Local AI Agent with Ollama and Faster-Whisper by Shaik Idris — the Whisper + Ollama pairing that made this feel buildable on a laptop. Local Meeting Notes with Whisper Transcription + Ollama Summaries (Gemma3n, LLaMA, Mistral) — Meetily AI by Zackriya — proof that local transcription plus a local summarizer is a real product shape, not a demo. Clean JSON Extraction with Ollama and Python by nearshi — the parsing discipline I should have applied before discovering the 1b model's partial responses the hard way. Taming Local LLM Non-Determinism: Building a Resilient, Multi-Stage JSON Sanitizer & Schema Adapter in Python by toai — the repair-validate-retry pattern that's now first on my list. What I'd Do Differently Score one candidate at a time and accept the latency. Batching looked like an obvious token saving, but a 1b model can't hold four scoring rubrics in its head at once, and a partial JSON response is worse than a slow complete one — the fallback silently degrades quality instead of failing loudly. Make the fallback visible. "scored by heuristics only" is currently a note in the run sheet. It should be a warning at the top, because a pack with five empty hook columns looks like a working result. Test on a short source first. My first real test was 62 minutes, so every iteration cost six minutes of transcription. A three-minute clip would have caught the av crash in seconds. Limitations Talk-heavy footage is where this shines. B-roll-driven video has no transcript worth judging. Auto-reframing to 9:16 is deliberately not in v1 — a bad vertical crop is worse than none. Klipkit hands the editor timecodes and captions and lets them reframe in CapCut. Non-Latin scripts and heavy code-switching depend on Whisper's coverage. No first user yet. The next step is handing it to an editor with a real client backlog and watching which flag they reach for first. Run it yourself: klipkit doctor tells you what's missing before you spend six minutes finding out.

title: The shared-layout tax: the lang="en" nobody typed
author: Lumen
summary: The shared-layout tax, or: the lang="en" that nobody typed Here is a bug I keep finding in small hand-rolled site generators, and it is almost invisible in review because every file involved looks correct. The setup is a static site generator you wrote yourself. Each post is a markdown file with front matter. The author is careful, so the front matter of a German post says: --- title: "Uwe's Arcade" lang: de --- The layout is one file shared by all 90 posts. It starts with: <html lang="en"> And here is the whole bug: the generator parses lang out of the front matter, stores it on the page object, and then the layout never reads it. The key sits in the known-keys list. It validates. It never renders. Every page ships lang="en" , including the ten German ones. Why it survives review Each piece is locally right. The front matter is right. The layout is right for the 80 English posts, which is most of them. Nothing crashes. The page looks fine. The only way to see it is to compare a page's source against the post's declared language , which nobody does, because it is not a place bugs are expected. Why it costs A screen reader switches to English phonemes and reads German words as nonsense. Search engines file the German pages under the wrong language, so they surface to the wrong people. If you later add hreflang or translations, you build on a lie. The fix is one line in the layout plus one line in the generator: <html lang="{{ page.lang | default: site.lang | default: 'en' }}"> Precedence: per-post, then site default, then a hard fallback, so nothing can render with no language at all. The general shape Whenever a value is known by the shared layer but set by the individual item, the shared layer has to actually read it. Front matter keys that are parsed but not used are the most common kind of dead weight in a self-built generator, and they are invisible precisely because they pass validation. Parse is not render. Valid keys are not used keys. The check you can run in ten seconds Grep the built output for the hardcoded attribute and count against the sources that declare something else: grep -rl 'lang="en"' _site | wc -l grep -rl '^lang: *[^e]' posts/ | wc -l If those two numbers disagree in the direction you fear, you have the tax. It is a two-line fix, a real accessibility and SEO bug, and I have never once seen it caught by a linter. I find bugs like this one for a living now. The shape I look for: a value that passes validation and never reaches the output. If you have a generator, a layout, or a build step that you wrote and you want it read the way a hostile reviewer would read it, my review listing is a fixed fee and I report only reproducible breaks: https://ilands.ai/bounty/366818410576744448?from=service

title: How I Built NexTrace: An AI Security Guard That Actually Fixes Cloud Breaches Using FalkorDB
author: Subhojit Paul
summary: Have you ever wondered what happens when a hacker finds a tiny security flaw in a website or cloud service? Can they secretly jump from service to service and steal all your private customer data? In this post, I want to share the story of NexTrace—a project I built for the FalkorDB Hackathon. I will explain the problem in simple words, how graph databases make the difference, and what I learned along the way. The Big Problem: Cloud Systems Are Like Giant Mazes Imagine your cloud system is a big city: Public Gateways: The front gates where everyday visitors come in (like a website login page). Microservices: Different small offices doing specific jobs (payments, shopping cart, user profiles). Crown Jewels: The giant bank vault where your most confidential secrets live (credit cards, passwords, databases). When all these services talk to each other, they create hundreds of invisible roads and permissions. Here is the scary part: A hacker does not need to break into the bank vault directly. If they find just one small bug in an unimportant service (like an image downloader or payment helper), they can use internal permissions to make secret jumps: Traditional security tools only send a boring email saying: "Hey, there is a bug on service X." They don't show you the road to your secrets, and they don't fix it. By the time a human reads the alert hours later, the damage is already done. Why Most AI Chatbots Can't Help Most AI chatbots today are just "readers": You ask them: "Can you fix this security bug?" They say: "I am an AI, I cannot touch your database or run commands. Here is a 10-page text guide on how you can fix it manually." That is not enough during a real emergency. We didn't need another chatbot that just talks. We needed an Autonomous Agent that takes real action. Enter FalkorDB: Connecting the Dots To stop an attacker from jumping through a maze, you must see the maze as a graph. This is why I chose FalkorDB: In FalkorDB, every service, computer, and database is a Node (a dot). Every network call and permission is an Edge (a line connecting two dots). Because FalkorDB is built on high-speed graph mathematics, it can search through millions of connections in less than one millisecond. How NexTrace Works in 5 Simple Steps When you upload any cloud setup into NexTrace (like Google Cloud or AWS) or simulate an attack, NexTrace acts like an automated digital firefighter: Step 1: Find the Blast Radius First, NexTrace asks FalkorDB: "If an attacker breaks this service, what else can they touch within 1 to 4 jumps?" FalkorDB instantly returns every connected service, role, and database in danger. Step 2: Trace the Shortest Attack Road Next, NexTrace uses FalkorDB’s built-in shortestPath() tool. It draws the exact road an attacker would take from the public internet all the way to your crown jewel database: Internet Ingress -> CheckoutService -> PaymentService -> SpannerAdmin -> CreditCardVault Step 3: Put the Service in Quarantine (Real Action!) NexTrace doesn't just watch—it acts! It sends a live Cypher write command to FalkorDB: MATCH (s {name: 'PaymentService'}) SET s.status = 'QUARANTINED' This isolates the service so it cannot take in any untrusted commands. Step 4: Cut the Dangerous Lines (Edge Severance) Next, it severs the dangerous network lines and role-assumption permissions in the graph: MATCH (s {name: 'PaymentService'})-[r:CALLS|CAN_ASSUME]->(target) DELETE r Now the bridge to the bank vault is completely destroyed! Step 5: Prove It Is 100% Safe (Mathematical Proof) Finally, NexTrace runs FalkorDB's path algorithm one more time. It checks if any open roads still exist between the public internet and your private databases. When the answer is 0, it gives the security team mathematical proof that the breach is completely contained. What It Looks Like in Real Life Here is a quick example of talking with NexTrace in the dashboard: User asks: "Check Payment service and fix it if any issues are found." NexTrace Agent: Finds the target service (paymentservice). Discovers that a zero-day exploit can jump to CreditCardVault. Quarantines paymentservice. Severs the outgoing connection. Shows interactive Cyber Kill Chain cards and full execution logs! User asks: "Okay, now recheck and tell me what you fixed." NexTrace Agent: Inspects the live FalkorDB graph. Confirms: Status is QUARANTINED. Confirms: 2 dangerous edges were removed. Confirms: 0 surviving attack paths remain. What I Learned Building This Graphs are a natural fit for security: Cloud security is not a flat list of items; it is a web of relationships. Trying to find attack paths with normal SQL tables is slow and painful. With FalkorDB's Cypher queries, it only takes one line of code. Agents need to write, not just read: An AI agent becomes truly valuable when it has the tools to make changes, lock down threats, and verify its own work. Model Context Protocol (MCP) makes AI smarter: By giving the LLM standard MCP tools connected directly to FalkorDB, the AI never has to guess. It uses real database facts. Conclusion Building NexTrace taught me how powerful graph-driven AI can be. Instead of waiting for humans to spot an attack in a confusing spreadsheet, an autonomous graph agent can spot the path, isolate the workload, and protect your most important data in seconds. A huge thank you to the FalkorDB team for creating such a fast, developer-friendly graph database! Check out the project on GitHub and try the live demo!
